# Handbook

This machine runs kitbash. Everything you can see through this connection lives in two places.

---
name: kitbash-single-container-limit
description: kitbash Packages support only one container unit per Package (v1); cross-Package traffic is HTTP-only via <name>.<member>.<domain>
metadata:
  type: project
---

kitbash v1 (`pkg_build`/`proc_run`) supports exactly one container unit per Package. There is no native docker-compose-style multi-container orchestration. Cross-Package communication only works through `expose: http` endpoints reachable at `https://<name>.<member>.<domain>` — there is no raw TCP exposure between Processes, so a backend that isn't HTTP (e.g. Redis speaking RESP on 6379) can't be split into its own Package and reached by another Package over that protocol.

**Why:** Confirmed by reading the `pkg_build`/`proc_run` tool descriptions ("Version 1 supports one container unit per Package" / "Version 1 runs the first container unit") and by inspecting existing packages: `bench-notes-dep` reaches `bench-cache-dep` via an env var pointing at its HTTP hostname, and the bench "cache" itself is a hand-rolled HTTP key-value server, not real Redis — because real Redis isn't HTTP-reachable across Packages here.

**How to apply:** When porting a multi-service docker-compose example (web + db/cache) into this kitbash workspace, bundle the backing service into the *same* container as the app (e.g. run `redis-server --daemonize yes` alongside the app process in one Dockerfile/CMD) rather than trying to create two Packages that talk over a raw port. Only split into separate Packages if the dependency can be swapped for an HTTP-speaking equivalent. See `/home/<member>/flask-redis` for a worked example (Flask + bundled `redis-server` in one container, upstream `docker/awesome-compose` flask-redis app code fetched unmodified via `git sparse-checkout`).
